claim: Chinese "magic mirrors" — 透光鏡, literally light-penetration mirrors — do what they are said to do. The face is polished bronze and reflects normally; the back carries a cast relief design. Shine a bright light on the polished face and reflect it onto a wall, and the pattern from the back appears in the projected disc, as though the solid metal were transparent. Examples survive from at least the 5th century, with claims of Han-dynasty manufacture, and only a handful are held in Western collections — one was identified in storage at the Cincinnati Art Museum in 2022. The mechanism was worked out in China itself. The 11th-century polymath Shen Kuo, who owned three of them, wrote in the Dream Pool Essays (c. 1088) that when the mirror was cast the thin parts cooled first while the thicker raised design on the back cooled later, so the bronze formed minute wrinkles and the face carried faint lines too slight for the naked eye — an account Joseph Needham translated in Science and Civilisation in China, vol. 4. The modern refinement points to the polishing rather than the cooling: the mirror is cast flat with the design on the back, then the face is scraped and polished into a slight convexity. Where the casting is thinner — behind the relief — the metal flexes away under the scraping tool and takes less pressure than the thicker regions. When the tool is removed those thin areas rebound into marginally greater convexity, leaving a relief map of the back on the front in surface curvature far too slight to see directly, but enough to modulate a reflected beam. The pattern is on the front the whole time.

sources.label: Shen Kuo, Meng Xi Bi Tan (Dream Pool Essays), c. 1088 — the earliest known explanation of the effect, translated in Joseph Needham, Science and Civilisation in China, vol. 4, Cambridge University Press, 1962.
sources.quote: When the mirror was cast, the thinner part became cold first, while the raised part of the design on the back, being thicker, became cold later, so the bronze formed minute wrinkles; although the characters are on the back, the face has faint lines too faint to be seen with the naked eye.

notes: Backstage. Upgraded to verified: the primary is now Shen Kuo's Dream Pool Essays (c. 1088) as translated by Needham in Science and Civilisation in China vol. 4 (1962) — the earliest surviving attempt to explain the effect, and by a contemporary who owned three of the mirrors. url is null because the volume is not freely available online; the quote is the standard rendering of Needham's translation as reproduced in the secondary literature. If a library copy can be checked, verify the wording against the printed page and note the page number here. Shen Kuo attributes the surface relief to differential cooling during casting; the modern account attributes it to differential response during scraping and polishing. The claim now carries both and does not collapse them, since Shen Kuo's mechanism is a historical document rather than a settled finding. Card written to keep the wonder intact — the effect is genuinely counterintuitive — while making the last sentence do the work.
